title: Comparing thresholds of XZZX and rotated surface codes under spatio-temporal correlated noise
abstract: While independent and identically distributed noise is typically assumed in quantum computing research, complex error models such as correlated and spatio-temporal errors remain underexplored. In this paper, the performance of $\mathrm{XZZX}$ and rotated surface codes is evaluated under these complex noise models. Standard graph-based decoders struggle with the hyperedges generated by correlated errors on bias-tailored codes. To address this, we employ the Minimum Weight Parity Factor (MWPF) decoder, which natively processes syndrome hypergraphs without artificial edge decomposition. Our simulations show that under strong Z-biased circuit-level correlated noise ($η=100$), the threshold of the rotated code degrades to $\approx 0.36\%$, while the $\mathrm{XZZX}$ code drops to $\approx 0.70\%$. Furthermore, a distinct non-monotonic threshold dependence is observed for the $\mathrm{XZZX}$ code across different bias ratios. While the $\mathrm{XZZX}$ code effectively absorbs high-density Z-type hyperedges at extreme biases, it exhibits a threshold minimum at moderate biases ($η\approx 10$) because transverse X and Y errors actively bridge the diagonal strings, breaking the code's one-dimensional decoupling symmetry. These findings demonstrate that utilizing hypergraph-aware decoders is critical, as the performance of bias-tailored codes is highly sensitive to the geometric structure of spatio-temporal correlated noise.
summary: This paper rigorously tests the performance of XZZX and rotated surface codes under realistic, correlated spatio-temporal noise, moving beyond simple i.i.d. error assumptions. By using a specialized hypergraph decoder, the authors demonstrate that the code's threshold is highly sensitive to the noise's geometric structure. The results highlight the necessity of accounting for correlated errors in the design of fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitations of assuming independent and identically distributed noise when evaluating quantum error correction codes.
main_result: The XZZX code outperforms the rotated surface code under strong Z-biased correlated noise, and its performance exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the noise bias ratio.
method: The study employs the Minimum Weight Parity Factor (MWPF) decoder to simulate code performance under complex, spatio-temporal correlated noise models.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on comparing the error thresholds of the XZZX and rotated surface codes, which are topological quantum error-correcting codes.
key_observables: Error threshold ($p_{th}$), logical error rate, and the dependence of performance on the noise bias ratio ($\eta$).
important_parameters: Noise bias ratio ($\eta$), code distance ($d$), and the strength of spatio-temporal correlations.
main_assumptions: Standard graph-based decoders fail when correlated errors generate syndrome hyperedges, necessitating the use of hypergraph-aware decoders.
figures_summary: Figures compare logical error rates vs. physical error rates, and plot the threshold physical error rate against the noise bias ratio ($\eta$) for both code types.
paper_structure: The paper evaluates code performance by first establishing the need for correlated noise models, then detailing the use of the MWPF decoder, and finally presenting comparative results showing the distinct threshold behaviors of the XZZX and rotated codes.
why_interesting: It provides concrete, quantitative results on how specific geometric structures of correlated noise break the assumptions underlying standard QEC analysis, which is crucial for designing fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

Fig. 3. Logical error rate vs. physical error rate under strongly Z-biased phenomenological noise (η = 100) for (left) Rotated Surface Code and (right) XZZX Surface Code, decoded using MWPF. Under this pure bias baseline, the XZZX code achieves a threshold of ≈7.40%, nearly 2.7× higher than the rotated code’s threshold of ≈2.70%, showcasing its high resilience to pure dephasing errors.

Fig. 4. Logical error rate vs. physical error rate under strongly Z-biased circuit-level noise (η = 100) for (left) Rotated Surface Code and (right) XZZX Surface Code, decoded using MWPF. Introducing circuit-level error propagation yields a threshold of ≈0.89% for the XZZX code and ≈0.71% for the rotated code, demonstrating that the XZZX code maintains a topological advantage under pure bias.

Fig. 5. Logical error rate vs. physical error rate under Z-biased phenomenological spatio-temporal correlated noise (η = 100) for (left) Rotated Surface Code and (right) XZZX Surface Code, decoded using MWPF. The introduction of correlated errors degrades the XZZX threshold to ≈1.86%, while the rotated code drops to ≈0.79%, illustrating the vulnerability of decoupled 1D chains to correlated noise.
